nameStory: Lovage gets its name from the old French word 'levesche,' which evolved from the Latin 'levisticum.' The Romans called it 'ligusticum' after Liguria, a region where they believed the best quality plants grew. Over time, 'lovage' became associated with love potions and romantic herbs in medieval folklore, though this connection came later and wasn't part of the original name.
description: Lovage is a tall, robust perennial herb that can tower over most garden plants, reaching 4-6 feet in height. It's a member of the carrot family with large, deeply divided leaves that look like giant celery leaves and small yellowish-green flowers arranged in umbrella-like clusters called umbels. This powerhouse herb has thick, hollow stems and produces an intensely aromatic fragrance that's like celery and parsley rolled into one, but much stronger. Originally from Afghanistan and Iran, it's now grown in gardens throughout New England as a culinary herb.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Large, glossy green leaves divided into wedge-shaped leaflets that look like oversized celery leaves. Crush a leaf between your fingers and you'll get an intense, spicy-sweet aroma that's unmistakably stronger than celery or parsley.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small yellowish-green flowers arranged in large, flat-topped umbrella clusters (umbels) typical of the carrot family. Each umbel contains dozens of tiny flowers that attract beneficial insects in mid to late summer.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: A tall, sturdy perennial that can reach 4-6 feet high with thick, hollow stems that feel substantial and fleshy when you squeeze them gently. The plant forms impressive clumps that return year after year.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Brown, oval seeds that look similar to fennel seeds but with a more intense, spicy-celery flavor when crushed. They're about 1/4 inch long with distinctive ridges running lengthwise.

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Large, fleshy taproot that's yellowish-white and gives off the same intense celery-like aroma as the leaves. The root system is substantial and helps anchor this tall plant.

habitat: In New England, lovage is almost exclusively found in cultivated gardens, herb gardens, and occasionally naturalized near old homesteads where it was once grown. It prefers rich, moist, well-drained soil and partial shade, thriving in the same conditions you'd find good garden vegetables. You won't find it growing wild in forests or fields, but it may persist for years around abandoned farmhouses or in neglected garden areas.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green shoots emerge early in spring, and young leaves can be harvested for their intense celery-like flavor. The plant grows rapidly once soil warms up.
seasonality.summer: Lovage reaches full height and produces its umbrella-like flower clusters in mid to late summer. This is when the plant is most impressive and easiest to identify from a distance.
seasonality.fall: Seeds ripen in early fall and can be collected for culinary use. Leaves begin to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: The entire above-ground portion dies back completely, leaving only the dormant root system underground. Nothing visible remains for identification.

funFact: Lovage was so prized by medieval monks that they grew it in every monastery garden and used every part of the plant - the leaves as medicine for stomach problems, the roots as vegetables, and the seeds as a spice that could substitute for expensive imported black pepper!
confusionNotes: Lovage is most often confused with angelica or large wild celery plants, but lovage's leaves are glossier and more wedge-shaped, and its aroma is much more intense - one whiff of crushed lovage leaves will immediately tell you it's something special, not just wild celery.
contextualKnowledge: Though lovage has 'love' in its name, it has nothing to do with romance - that's just how the old French word evolved into English. Don't confuse this garden herb with any wild carrot family plants you might find in nature, as that family includes some dangerously poisonous species like poison hemlock.
compareHints: Lovage is the only species in its genus, making it unique among carrot family plants. Compared to other large carrot family herbs like angelica, lovage has glossier, more deeply divided leaves and a distinctly spicy-celery aroma rather than angelica's sweeter, more medicinal scent. Unlike wild carrot family plants, lovage is robust and garden-worthy with thick, substantial stems.
